title: Is it an arthritis flare or something else? Warning signs and who to call (UK guide)

content:
When someone with arthritis suddenly cannot get out of a chair, walk or manage the stairs, it is easy to blame a flare. Often it is a flare, but sometimes the joints are not the real problem. An infection such as a urine or chest infection, a joint infection, gout, polymyalgia rheumatica, a medicine side effect, dehydration, a fall or a stroke can all look like 'arthritis playing up' in an older person. A flare usually affects joints you already know about, in a familiar way, and slowly settles with your flare plan. Get help quickly if someone becomes suddenly confused, has a fever or feels shivery, has one hot, swollen and very painful joint, cannot put weight on a leg, has new weakness on one side or slurred speech, or simply seems much more unwell than usual. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

This guide is for the moment you are unsure whether it is "just a flare". If you already know it is a flare and want to manage it, see what to do in an arthritis flare or, for rheumatoid or other inflammatory arthritis in later life, getting through a flare week.

What a typical flare looks like

  • It affects joints that have flared before, or the same pattern of joints.
  • Pain, stiffness, warmth or swelling build up over hours or days rather than seconds.
  • You may feel tired and low, but you are still yourself: clear-headed, eating and drinking, and able to do some things.
  • Your usual flare plan (rest and gentle movement, heat or cold, pain relief your GP or pharmacist has agreed, the rheumatology advice line if you have one) starts to help within a few days.

If that sounds right, follow your plan and see flare-ups. Keep a short note of what is happening so you can tell your GP or team if it does not settle.

Signs it may be something else

In older people, many illnesses first show up as "can't get going", more falls or a sudden drop in what someone can do, rather than the symptoms you might expect. Think beyond the joints if you notice:

  • Sudden confusion, drowsiness or someone "not being themselves". The NHS says infections, especially urine infections, are a common cause in older people. Sudden confusion needs medical help immediately.
  • A fever, or feeling hot, cold or shivery.
  • One joint that is suddenly hot, swollen, red and very painful, especially with a temperature or if you have a joint replacement or rheumatoid arthritis. This can be septic arthritis (a joint infection) or gout, and needs checking the same day.
  • New pain and stiffness in both shoulders, the neck or the hips, worst in the morning, in someone over 50. This can be polymyalgia rheumatica. A new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain when chewing or any change in vision alongside it can mean giant cell arteritis, which is an emergency for your eyesight.
  • Sudden weakness or numbness on one side, a drooping face or slurred speech. These are signs of a stroke: call 999.
  • Not being able to put weight on a leg after a fall, or new pain in the hip or groin after a fall, even a small one.
  • A change after a new or changed medicine, such as dizziness, drowsiness, constipation or confusion. Tell your GP or pharmacist; do not stop the medicine yourself.
  • Not eating or drinking much, a dry mouth or passing very little urine, which can point to dehydration or an infection.

Who to call

  • Call 999 or go to A&E for stroke signs, sudden confusion, severe breathing problems, signs of sepsis (for example very cold or blotchy skin, very fast breathing, or someone hard to wake), or if someone may have broken a bone.
  • Get an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 the same day for one hot, swollen, very painful joint, a fever with joint pain, new shoulder and hip girdle stiffness, or symptoms of a urine infection.
  • Call your rheumatology advice line if you have inflammatory arthritis and it looks like a flare that is not settling. NICE NG100 says people with rheumatoid arthritis should have rapid access to specialist care for flares.
  • See your GP routinely if things have been slowly getting harder over weeks or months. A gradual slow-down is worth a review too, including a medicines review, blood tests and a check of strength, balance and mood.

Write it down before you call

Whoever you speak to will find it easier to help if you can say:

  • when it started and whether it came on suddenly or slowly
  • which joints, or whether it is more of an all-over feeling
  • whether there is a temperature, confusion, a fall, or a change in eating, drinking or passing urine
  • any new, stopped or changed medicines
  • what the person could do last week compared with today

After an illness or a long flare

A few days in bed or in a chair can take a lot of strength away, especially later in life. Once the cause has been treated, start moving little and often and build back up. See getting your strength back after a flare or illness. If you are falling or nearly falling, ask your GP about the local falls service.

For family and carers

You often notice the change first. Trust that feeling if someone seems different from their usual self. A person who is confused may not be able to tell you how unwell they feel, so look for fever, not drinking, new incontinence or not being able to get up. If in doubt, ask NHS 111 or, for sudden confusion, call 999.

Common questions

Can a urine infection make arthritis feel worse?

It can make someone feel weak, achy and much less able to move, and in older people it can cause sudden confusion without the usual burning or stinging. If someone is suddenly confused, get medical help immediately.

Is it a flare if only one joint is very hot and swollen?

It might be, but a single hot, swollen, very painful joint can also be gout or a joint infection. Get it checked the same day, especially if you feel unwell or have a temperature.

Should I wait a few days to see if it settles?

Only if it looks like your usual flare and none of the warning signs above are there. If you are not sure, ask NHS 111 or your rheumatology advice line rather than waiting.

If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111.
